sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video generation models now produce realistic footage from text prompt or single image. However, visual realism alone does not ensure consistent 3D geometry, physically plausible dynamics, or temporal coherence (Huang et al., 2024; Bansal et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026a; Ying et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026c). In game development, film previsualization, and agent-driven content creation, creators often specify the scene layout, object motion, and camera trajectory in advance. Designers block out scenes, animators key character motion, and coding agents script camera paths. These structural priors turn the task into rendering: producing realistic video that follows the specified scene and its evolution. With geometry and dynamics specified by these priors, the video model can focus on appearance synthesis, reducing the scope for structural and temporal drift. Recent systems therefore link executable world state to video generation through proxy videos (Chen et al., 2026b) or engine buffers (Zhan et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a), so that the engine determines scene evolution and video model renders it. Building such renderer still faces three problems. First, control is tied to fixed set of representations. Engine-driven renderers are built around the one representation their engine exports, such as white-box frames (Zhan et al., 2026), semantic maps (Lu et al., 2026d), proxy videos (Chen et al., 2026b), or full G-buffers (Lin et al., 2026a), and general controllable generators attach branch per condition (Zhang et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025) or label the type of each input (Mao et al., 2026), so new engine or new kind of proxy calls for new model. Second, rendering is slow. large video backbone needs tens of denoising steps, and distilling structure-conditioned model of this size from scratch is costly (Lin et al., 2026a), which keeps such renderers far from interactive use. Third, training pairs are rarely aligned frame by frame. Conditions estimated from real videos carry estimator errors and differ from engine proxies (Xu et al., 2026), and engine-paired data so far come from single engine. We present , which adapts frozen MiniMax-H3 33B Ref2VA backbone (MiniMax, 2026) and addresses the three problems in turn (Figure 2). For omni-structure control, structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone, each structural latent takes the RoPE (Su et al., 2021) position of the target frame it describes, and no reference carries type identifier, as each representation is described in plain text instead, so that single control LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) follows block-outs, semantic maps, shaded geometry, and body meshes alike. For fast rendering, we post-train pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone with structure-guided distribution matching, which extends distribution matching distillation (Yin et al., 2024b) with teacher extrapolated along the structural condition, so that the model renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling while preserving the learned control. block-causal variant of the same design further streams 768p video in real time. For frame-aligned supervision, we collect 136K clips from eight sources whose structure is exported by game engines and simulators or fitted to YouTube videos, so that each structural frame matches its target frame in both content and timing. We evaluate on an in-distribution test set with ground-truth videos and on generalization benchmark that covers 16 structural representations, 11 of them unseen in training. The results show that our four-step model outperforms existing acceleration LoRAs and the official backbone, surpasses existing structure-conditioned renderers, and achieves new state of the art in structure-conditioned video rendering. Notably, our method shows strong generalization to unseen structure. It faithfully renders pose skeletons, pencil storyboards, childrens crayon drawings, wireframes, and point clouds, none of which appears in training. Our contributions are fourfold: We present renderer that handles any structural representation with single control LoRA through the native reference pathway, without type identifiers or added branches. We propose structure-guided distribution matching, which post-trains pretrained four-step LoRA so that our model renders in four steps while preserving its structural control. We build frame-aligned paired corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos, in which every structural frame is aligned with its target frame. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on an in-distribution test set and generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations, including 11 unseen in training, and its causal variant renders 768p video in real time.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Rendering Engine and Agent State into Video. World modeling encompasses 3D and 4D scene generation (Kong et al., 2025) and interactive proxies that provide feedback for agent learning (Yang et al., 2026b). Recent systems let game engine, simulator, or coding agent decide what happens in scene and let video model render it. Most of them train renderer on one structural representation exported by their engine, such as white-box frames (Zhan et al., 2026; Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026), semantic maps (Lu et al., 2026d), depth and normal maps (Chi et al., 2026), projected 3D boxes (Huang et al., 2026b), or the proxy video of code world model (Chen et al., 2026b; Liao and Liu, 2026), and several distill the renderer to few streaming steps for real-time use (VAST-AI-Research, 2026; Lu et al., 2026d). related branch renders from full G-buffers that also carry materials and lighting (Zeng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026c; Liang et al., 2025). Other works avoid paired proxy data, either by learning from posed RGB-D video (Xu et al., 2026) or by showing proxy renders to frozen model during the early denoising steps only (Liang et al., 2026). However, each renderer is built around the representation of its own engine, so new engine or new kind of proxy calls for new renderer. follows many kinds of structure with single control LoRA, including structure it has never seen. Structure-Conditioned Video Generation. Controllable video generation commonly injects conditions in one of two ways. Branch-based methods attach trainable copy or added control blocks to the backbone, from ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023) to multi-condition variants on video backbones (Alibaba PAI, 2026; NVIDIA, 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). Sequence-based methods place condition tokens next to the target tokens and read them with full attention, often through small LoRA (Tan et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). Further works steer generation through warped noise, 3D tracking videos, reference videos, predicted LoRAs, or jointly generated intrinsic channels (Burgert et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b), and training-free methods condition an existing model through structured first frames or ControlNet-style world model (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). However, these methods add parameters for control, label the type of each condition, or are trained on fixed set of condition kinds. passes an untyped structural video through the native reference pathway of the backbone with one LoRA, so that the same model also follows structure unseen in training. Few-Step Distillation and Acceleration Adapters. Few-step video generation is usually obtained in two ways. One distills multi-step teacher into few-step student by distribution matching (Yin et al., 2024b,a; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026) or consistency and flow-map distillation (Zheng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026). The other trains plug-in acceleration LoRA once on base model and attaches it to models derived from the same base (Luo et al., 2023; Lin and Yang, 2024; Yang et al., 2026a; Hao AI Lab, 2026), with recent work making such LoRAs transferable between base and distilled models (Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b). For conditional models, several works distill the conditional model itself or re-tune its control module after distillation (Wang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2026), and MotionEcho (Rong et al., 2025) restores motion control at inference with guidance from the slow teacher. However, distilling large control model from scratch is costly, and generic few-step adapter attached unchanged lowers the visual quality and first-frame fidelity of the control model. post-trains four-step LoRA on the frozen control model, with distribution-matching teacher extrapolated toward its structure-conditioned prediction. 3 : Native Reference Rendering turns pretrained video backbone into renderer by adding only lightweight adapters. In this section, we formulate the rendering task and outline the design (Section 3.1), describe how structural references are aligned with the target and described in text (Section 3.2), and present the two-stage training of control and acceleration (Section 3.3), followed by its causal streaming extension (Section 3.4).

sections.title:
3.2 Frame-Aligned Reference Conditioning
Native Reference Pathway. A renderer must match every structural frame with the target frame it describes.
Instead of attaching a ControlNet branch (Zhang et al., 2023) or concatenating channels, both of which
introduce parameters trained from scratch, we feed the structural video and the optional first frame
through the reference pathway of the backbone (MiniMax, 2026). This pathway packs text, reference
videos, audio, and the target video into one full-attention sequence (Figure 2), so the control adapter can
inherit the pretrained ability to read reference videos. We refer to the tokens of the supplied references as
reference tokens and to those of the generated video as target tokens. Yet native reference tokens occupy
a separate temporal segment before the clip and their own spatial grid, so the zero-shot backbone uses a
structural video as a loose reference and copies it or changes the camera instead of following the structure.
sections.content: Frame-Aligned Positional Encoding. Since rotary position embedding (Su et al., 2021) makes attention depend on the relative offset between tokens, we supply the missing correspondence through positions. Each reference token receives the RoPE coordinates of the target token it describes. The k-th structural latent frame shares the temporal index and spatial grid of the k-th target latent frame, and the first frame is encoded as static clip at index 0 (Figure 2). Tokens at the same position remain distinguishable through their timesteps, as reference tokens keep the near-clean value that the backbone assigns to reference inputs while target tokens carry the current noise level. This extends shared positions for aligned 4 image conditions (Tan et al., 2025) to temporally aligned video and, like in-context control of video models without structural changes (Fang et al., 2025), requires no additional module. Untyped References with Fixed Descriptions. Structural representations from different sources constrain different aspects of the target (Section 4.1). We keep reference tokens untyped in the sequence, without type identifier or modality embedding, so the adapter infers what reference constrains from the structural video itself. The prompt additionally describes each representation with two fixed sentences, definition of what it shows and rule that names the attributes to follow and the visual properties that must not appear. For scene block-out: <Video 1> is an untextured grey block-out of the scene, rendered from the same camera as the target video, giving the layout, the large geometry, the characters bodies, their motion and the camera of every frame. <Video 1> (frame-by-frame layout, geometry, motion and camera): attribute_transfer - the layout, large shapes, character bodies, motion and camera are followed exactly; small objects, materials, colours and lighting are not given by <Video 1> and are the target videos own; the grey look of <Video 1> is not shown. The same representation always receives the same sentences. Open-vocabulary text describes each representation, so new format needs only new description, with no added parameters or retraining.

sections.title: 3.4 Causal Streaming Extension
sections.content: To generate video incrementally, we extend the same two-stage design to block-causal attention. The clip is split into blocks of at most five latent frames. We adapt the bidirectional control LoRA with teacher forcing so that each block attends to the prompt, the first frame, the structure of itself and the five preceding blocks, and the clean frames of the five preceding blocks, never to later block. We then freeze this causal control LoRA and post-train separate acceleration LoRA, initialized from the bidirectional four-step LoRA, on the students own block-by-block rollouts, with the bidirectional control model as the structure-guided teacher (w = 1.5). Each rollout is generated without gradients and replayed as one teacher-forced sequence, so that the gradient reaches both how each block is generated and how it serves as 6 context for later blocks. At inference, we merge the acceleration LoRA into the backbone, keep the control LoRA attached, sample each block in four steps, and update the fixed-window keyvalue cache before outputting the block immediately. With streaming VAE decoder (Chen et al., 2026a) that decodes each block without future latents, the causal model renders 768p video in real time at up to 28 FPS.

sections.title: 4 Engine-Aligned Paired Data
sections.content: A renderer learns to follow structure only from pairs in which the target video actually follows the structure. Conditions estimated from real videos, such as predicted depth or segmentation, carry the errors of the estimator and differ from the engine proxies that the renderer receives at test time. We therefore collect pairs whose condition is exported by an engine or fitted to the target, and use pair as structural supervision only when its condition matches the target in time and carries enough structure. We then describe the data sources (Section 4.1), the checks that decide how each source is used (Section 4.2), and the construction of prompts (Section 4.3).

sections.title: 4.1 Data Sources
sections.content: The training set contains 136K samples, about 243 hours of video. Every clip is 158-frame window at 24 fps and 768p resolution. The data cover diverse sources and control types (Figure 3), listed below with the condition each one supplies. Magpie (Zhan et al., 2026) records human-played Unreal Engine gameplay across many scenes at 60 fps, together with synchronized grey block-out of the scene. The block-out gives the layout, the large geometry, the bodies and motion of the characters, and the camera of every frame, while materials and lighting are left to the model. CARLA (Dosovitskiy et al., 2017) provides urban and rural driving. Among the buffers that the simulator exports, we use semantic segmentation, which paints every class in one flat colour and thus specifies the class layout of the scene without its appearance. Engine recordings consist of frames together with depth, object masks, camera poses, and skeletons on shared timestamps. We render the depth as grey shading, with distant regions and the sky set to black, so that it conveys the shape of the scene near the camera. Blender renders of animated scenes are paired with the white-box of their scene, which describes the scene layout and the motion of the main character. UnrealZoo (Zhong et al., 2025) provides Unreal Engine 5 environments in firstand third-person views. Its condition combines object masks and skeletons, with one colour per object and the skeleton of each character drawn on top. YouTube videos (Ju et al., 2024) provide clips for body-motion conditioning. We keep videos with clear protagonist, fit the SMPL body (Loper et al., 2015) of the protagonist with GVHMR (Shen et al., 2024) using camera and depth from VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a) and Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2026b), and render it from the target camera as grey body on white background. This SMPL body video gives the position, pose, and motion of the protagonist, while the environment and clothing come from the first frame and text. WildWorld (Li et al., 2026c), public dataset of Monster Hunter Wilds gameplay, and OmniWorld (Zhou et al., 2026), which collects footage of AAA games such as Cyberpunk 2077, contribute rich game appearance. Their structural annotations follow the frames less closely, so we use them as appearance data and supply only first frame.

sections.title: 4.2 Data Checks
sections.content: A condition can fail in two ways. It can be offset from the target in time or space, or it can be aligned yet too coarse to describe the target. We therefore run two checks on every source. Temporal and Spatial Agreement. For timing, we correlate the motion of each condition with that of its target over range of frame offsets. The offset at which the correlation peaks shows whether the two are synchronized, and clips whose peak is not at zero offset are removed. For space, we measure the recall of the condition edges in the target frame and compare it with the recall of the horizontally mirrored condition. condition that matches its target recovers clearly more edges than its mirror, so clips without this margin are removed as spatially misaligned. For the data, we first used box proxies that draw body parts and objects as coarse boxes. 4.3 Prompts and Input Combinations
Captions. Each caption follows the six-section prompt format of the backbone, which consists of subject
definitions, a summary with a task prefix, a retention analysis, a detailed description, the soundscape,
and the music (Figure 2). Two parts fill these sections. 1 A scene description covers materials, colours,
illumination, weather, character appearance, events, camera motion, and sound, and fills the summary,
the detailed description, the soundscape, and the music. Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot AI, 2026; Kimi Team,

definitions, names the task in the summary prefix, and states in the retention analysis which attributes of
each reference the output follows. Code generates it from the input combination of the clip (Section 3.2),
so the description of each condition stays identical across clips.
sections.content: Input Combinations. The training samples mix four input combinations, with 67.1% supplying structure and first frame, 16.7% structure only, 13.2% first frame only, and 2.9% text only. Sources with structure also contribute some samples without it, so that missing structure is not tied to the appearance of WildWorld and OmniWorld. The combination of each clip is fixed when the data is built, and its prompt describes exactly the supplied inputs. Dropping the structure at random during training would leave prompt that still refers to it, so fixing the combination in advance prevents the absent input from leaking through the prompt.

sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: We ablate the post-training stage on the generalization benchmark with Gemini Elo ratings (Tables 2 and 3), and the conditioning design and the training data scored by automatic metrics (Tables 4 and 5). Comparison with Existing Acceleration LoRAs. An existing four-step LoRA attached to our control LoRA renders in four steps, but it was trained without the control adapter and shifts the outputs of the control model. Composed this way, LongLive-Plug, DMAD, and FastH3 reach overall ratings of 922, 1006, and 1053  (Table 3)  . Structure-guided post-training removes the mismatch and lifts the DMAD start to 1096, above every composition, with the highest quality and first-frame ratings. The gain therefore comes from adapting the acceleration LoRA to the control model. Structure Guidance. Table 2 post-trains the same students without guidance (w = 1), either by updating the four-step LoRA from DMAD or LongLive-Plug, or by self-distillation, which updates the control LoRA with LongLive-Plug frozen. Plain distribution matching pulls the student toward teacher whose structure-conditioned prediction is blurry, so the unguided student degrades its starting point, from 1024 to 820 for DMAD and from 1028 to 798 for LongLive-Plug. Extrapolating the teacher along the structural condition sharpens this target, and the guided student rates far above both the unguided student and its start from every starting point, 1156 against 820 from DMAD, 1107 against 798 from LongLive-Plug, and 1066 against 949 with self-distillation, with the best value on almost every judge question. blind human comparison with the unguided DMAD student agrees in direction. Starting Point and Strength. Guidance improves every starting point, and DMAD with = 1.5 gives the best student. The best strength depends on the start. From LongLive-Plug, = 2 is better than = 1.5 (1107 against 1067 in Table 2), whereas from DMAD, = 2 lowers the rating from 1096 to 1045  (Table 3)  . 12 Figure 8 gallery of structure-conditioned renderings. Each image comes from different case, spanning human motion, everyday scenes, and imagined environments across seen and unseen structural representations. Schedule, Training Length, and Sampling Steps. Applying guidance only at re-noising levels σ 0.9 rates on par with guidance at every level (1107 against 1096), so guidance acts mainly at high noise levels, where the layout of the clip is decided. Longer post-training does not help, as 1,200 iterations lower the overall rating to 992, and adding self-distillation of the control LoRA on top of our post-training lowers it to 13 1049. The student is trained for four steps and works best with four. Two steps lower the overall rating to 961, and eight steps bring no gain (1080). Conditioning Design. Table 4 trains variants of the control model under the same data and budget. ControlNet branch in place of the native reference pathway lowers the structure score from 48.0 to 46.8 and the stability, and giving the structure tokens separate RoPE positions instead of those of their target frames lowers quality and structure, which supports native reference conditioning. Reading the structure at full instead of half resolution further raises the structure score from 46.6 to 48.0. Frame-Aligned Data. Table 5 varies the training data. Using the WildWorld boxes, which do not line up with the frames, as structure lowers the structure score from 47.4 to 46.6, since misaligned supervision teaches the model to loosen its control. Training only on samples with structure lowers stability. The final corpus therefore keeps samples without structure for appearance and uses as structure only sources whose structure is aligned frame by frame with the video. Training on 1/10 of the data changes every score by at most 0.2, less than retraining on the full data with new seed, whereas removing the misaligned structure helps more, so the alignment of the data matters more than its amount.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented , few-step generative renderer that turns structure from game engines and coding agents into realistic video. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of frozen MiniMax-H3 backbone without any type identifier, so that single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations, and structure-guided distribution matching adapts pretrained four-step LoRA to this control model. Trained on 136K frame-aligned clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on both the in-distribution test set and the generalization benchmark, and generalizes to representations never seen in training, while rendering 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling. Its block-causal variant further renders 768p video in real time.

The control LoRA has rank 384 on the attention and feed-forward layers and is trained with the native flow-matching objective of the backbone on clips of 158 frames at 1344 768 and 24 fps, using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate of 104 for 38,400 steps at batch of 4. For structure-guided post-training, the control LoRA is frozen and the teacher is the backbone with the control LoRA. The four-step LoRA has rank 384, with its first 128 ranks initialized from the pretrained DMAD LoRA and the rest at zero, and the fake-score model is separate LoRA initialized at the teacher. The generator is updated once every five fake-score updates, with learning rates of 105 for the generator and 2 106 for the fake-score model, for 800 iterations at batch of 4 with = 1.5. The conditioning and data ablations use an earlier data mixture. The causal control LoRA (Section 3.4) starts from the control LoRA after 38,400 steps and is trained with teacher forcing for 19,200 steps at batch of 2, using AdamW with learning rate of 3 105. The four-step model also improves on Stage 1 on all four questions, showing that the benefit of structure-guided post-training extends to representations absent from the training corpus. It also leads the total automatic score at 70.6, followed by Stage 1 at 70.4. Pairwise Comparison with Existing Methods. Figure 15 reports the normalized winloss margin of ours against each method, complementing the ratings in Table 1. Every margin is nonnegative on both test sets. Against LynnReal-Omni, the overall comparison is even on the generalization benchmark, but the structure margin reaches +0.27, and all four questions favor ours on the in-distribution test set. Against Stage 1, quality improves alongside structure and first-frame preservation on both sets. These direct comparisons support the same conclusion as the Elo ratings: four-step rendering improves the controlled output, with the strongest gain over the closest external competitor in structure. Results by Representation and Source. Figure 16 expands the categories in Figure 6 into individual representations and sources. Bold rows match the categories in Figure 6, with individual representations and sources below. Positive values favor ours. every broad group, with particularly strong results on pose inputs and shaded geometry. Against our 50-step Stage 1 model, the four-step model wins on six of eight agent-built skeleton cases and on six of seven silhouettes, but loses on colour-mapped depth, voxels, and pencil storyboards. Thus, the gains on unseen inputs cover several distinct formats, while some individual formats still favor full-step sampling. The category totals and the case counts make both patterns visible beyond the aggregate comparison. Comparison on Automatic Metrics. Table 8 compares quality, stability, control, and first-frame preservation on both test sets. Our method has the highest total on the in-distribution test set and matches Stage 1 at the reported precision on the generalization benchmark. Individual renderers lead different groups: LynnReal-Omni leads quality, Cosmos-Transfer2.5 and Wan2.2-VACE-Fun lead control on the two sets, and Streaming CWM leads stability but has the lowest control scores. Our model balances quality and structural agreement. Compared with Stage 1, post-training improves control on both sets and quality on the in-distribution test set, while stability and first-frame preservation decrease. These changes leave the generalization total nearly unchanged and raise the in-distribution total. Visual Comparison with Other Methods. Figure 17 summarizes comparisons on 86 demonstration cases from 15 works. We render each case using the structural input shared on its project page and the provided first frame, or the first frame of its output video when no separate reference is available. We compare our outputs with the original results, presenting each pair to the judge in both orders. The comparison covers StreamRender-H3, Magpie, Cosmos-Transfer2.5, SceneCraft, Proxy2World, Diffusion as Shader, PAI ControlNet-Union, Programmable World Model, the neural rendering examples of Safka (2026), Go-with-the-Flow, VACE, EdenLive, CWM, AgentGarten, and Code Video Model. Across these cases, ours wins 49 comparisons, ties 13, and loses 24, giving net score of +0.29. The positive margin shows that our model also competes well on cases selected by other methods. Table 9 supplements Table 2 with automatic scores. Guidance improves quality and control from every starting point, consistent with teacher that more strongly follows the structural input. From the DMAD start, control rises from 59.2 to 61.0 and quality from 68.0 to 69.1, while stability and first-frame preservation fall. These changes slightly lower the equally weighted total, even as the pairwise ratings improve. The automatic groups expose this tradeoff, while the higher Elo ratings reflect the judges joint preference over appearance and structure. Post-Training and Sampling Settings. Table 10 gives group scores for the settings in Table 3. Post-training the DMAD composition raises quality and control, while its lower stability and first-frame score reduce the automatic total. Increasing guidance to = 2 further lowers stability with little change in control. Eight sampling steps improve quality slightly over four, but reduce first-frame preservation and leave the total unchanged at the reported precision. Two steps have the highest control score but lower first-frame score. Four steps achieve the highest overall, quality, and first-frame Elo ratings among these settings, balancing rendering quality with sampling cost. Conditioning Design. Table 7 collects the group scores of Tables 4 and 5 and adds their automatic totals. The native full-resolution pathway improves stability and control over the ControlNet branch, with small reduction in quality. Increasing structural resolution raises control from 46.6 to 48.0 and the total from 66.2 to 66.5, with little change in the other groups. At half resolution, shared RoPE also improves quality and control over separate positions. The consistent control gains support aligning reference tokens with the target frames and preserving the spatial detail of the structural input. Training Data. The lower block of Table 7 compares data variants. Keeping only structured samples raises control but lowers stability and first-frame preservation, leaving the automatic total unchanged at the reported precision. Removing misaligned structural supervision improves quality, stability, and control over using all data, raising the total from 66.2 to 66.5. The corpus therefore benefits from combining reliable structural supervision with appearance-only samples. Reducing the data to one tenth has smaller effect than the variation between full-data runs, consistent with prioritizing alignment over data volume.
